schools.summary: Ellicott separates the two phrases naming those summoned, taking the elders for chiefs of official rank such as the princes and counsellors of the king and the heads of the tribes for the feudal chiefs of the great families, and notes that these alone were specially summoned while the rest assembled without summons because the dedication was blended with the Feast of Tabernacles; Keil and Delitzsch stand back from the detail and set out the threefold structure of the whole chapter.

Clarke explains the delay by the calendar, that Solomon deferred the dedication to the year after the temple was finished because that year was a jubilee, and lays the fortnight out day by day from the first of the seven days of dedication to the return home.
Gill hesitates over the word elders, taking them for the judges in the several cities or the senators of the great sanhedrim, and adds that it is a question whether as yet there was such a court.

debates.question: Who exactly was summoned?
debates.positions: Ellicott distinguishes the elders from the heads of the tribes, against the old Greek version which identifies them, and assigns the first to official and the second to feudal rank; Gill leaves the term unsettled between civic judges and a senate whose existence at this date he doubts.

outliers.view: Dates the whole ceremony by a jubilee year and sets out the fourteen days hour by hour, down to which day of the week each fell on.

themes: Solomon assembled the elders of Israel
the city of David, which is Zion

schools.summary: Keil and Delitzsch canvass three explanations of the name of the month and keep the first, that it means the month of the flowing brooks, rejecting the equinox on the ground that the plural form does not favour it and rejecting the month of gifts along with the dating that supports it, since the month answers rather to the period between the new moon of October and that of November, when the rainy season commences; Ellicott takes the rejected view, that it means the month of gifts, as bringing with it the gathering of the vintage.

Gill denies that the feast named is the feast of tabernacles, though that fell in the same month, holding it to be the feast of the dedication kept before it, since the two together lasted fourteen days and the people were dismissed on the twenty-third; and he describes the crowd, a vast number of common people come to see the solemnity.
Clarke says flatly that it was the feast of tabernacles, celebrated in the seventh month of the ecclesiastical year.

debates.question: What does the name of the month mean?
debates.positions: Keil and Delitzsch argue for the flowing brooks and against both the equinox and the month of gifts, reasoning from the plural form and from when the rains actually begin; Ellicott adopts the month of gifts, from the gathering in of the vintage and the last of the crops, and reports from the old Targum that it once began the civil year.

debates.question: Which feast was it?
debates.positions: Clarke and Ellicott take it for the feast of tabernacles, Ellicott adding that the transference of the ark to a fixed habitation was peculiarly appropriate to the most joyful feast of the year; Gill denies the identification and makes it the feast of the dedication, which was kept before the other, arguing from the total of fourteen days and the date of the dismissal.

outliers.view: Stands alone against the other witnesses on which feast is meant, and argues it from the arithmetic of the fortnight rather than from the month.

schools.summary: Ellicott settles who was entitled to carry the ark from the distribution of offices, that bearing it on its journeys belonged to the Levites of the family of Kohath but taking it out of the Holy of Holies and replacing it was the work of the priests alone, and finds the narrative literally accurate in its sequence; he also holds that the question which tent was brought up need not be decided, since each section of priests and Levites probably brought up what was entrusted to it; Keil and Delitzsch read the clause about the Levites as a supplementary notice rather than a second act, and identify the tent of meeting definitely as the Mosaic tabernacle at Gibeon.

Henry explains the difference from the wilderness arrangement, that there the Levites carried the ark because there were not priests enough, whereas here, this being the last time it was to be carried, the priests did it themselves as they had been ordered to do at Jericho.

Clarke reports the two tabernacles and declines to choose, noting that some think both were brought in to prevent the danger of idolatry, though he would rather suppose that the one from Gibeon was brought in and the temporary one demolished.
Gill states only the bare movement, that they brought up the ark from the city of David to the temple.

debates.question: Which tent was brought into the temple?
debates.positions: Keil and Delitzsch are definite for the Mosaic tabernacle at Gibeon, arguing that the tent on Zion can be proved never to have been so designated and that another account distinguishes them; Clarke reports the same two candidates and declines to decide, inclining to Gibeon; Ellicott sidesteps the question by supposing each body of Levites brought up its own charge.

outliers.view: Closes with the Jewish tradition that the prophet hid the tabernacle and the ark and the altar of incense by miracle at the destruction of the temple, offered as a possible trace of where the disused furniture was stored.

themes: the priests took up the ark

schools.summary: Ellicott sets the inaugural sacrifice beside the ceremonial of the day when David brought up the ark to Zion and leaves open whether it was offered as the ark left Zion or on its arrival; Keil and Delitzsch place it on arrival, in the court or before the hall, and draw from the detail that the shade covered the poles as well as the ark an inference about how the ark stood, that its poles ran north and south rather than east and west, correcting their own earlier sketch.

Gill adds that the place in the oracle answered to what the ark had had in the tabernacle and that the wings spread from wall to wall, and rejects both the view that the poles were lengthened for the larger house and the view that they were drawn wholly out and laid up, holding that they were drawn out only some little way.

Clarke takes the closing phrase for evidence about the book rather than the furniture, that the poles being there unto this day proves the account was written before the destruction of the first temple, though how long before we cannot tell.

debates.question: Were new and longer poles made for the temple?
debates.positions: Keil and Delitzsch refuse the rendering that would say so, arguing that the tense cannot be pluperfect here and that on that reading the object would be marked by the usual particle, the verb being intransitive and meaning to be long; Gill rejects the same opinion on the different ground that the poles were not made larger merely because the house was larger.

outliers.view: Use the shadow of the cherubim over the poles to fix the orientation of the ark, and correct a diagram of their own on the strength of it.

themes: under the wings of the cherubims
the ends of the staves were seen
there they are unto this day

schools.summary: Ellicott calls the emphasis on what the ark did not contain remarkable and takes it as meant to show that the pot of manna, the rod and the copy of the Law were beside the ark and not in it, and holds that this clear statement must determine the interpretation of the well-known passage in the Epistle, where no stress need be laid on the word wherein; Keil and Delitzsch give the remark a narrower purpose, to show that the law about what the ark should preserve had not been departed from in the lapse of time.

Gill reads the exclusion as covering writings only, or as one rabbi has it the rest of the law as distinct from the decalogue, and offers a grammatical escape from the difficulty, that the particle rendered there may equally be rendered at or with or by, so that the rod and the pot might have stood on the sides of the ark.

debates.question: Were the rod and the pot of manna inside the ark?
debates.positions: Gill keeps the possibility open by construing the preposition loosely, so that they might have stood at or by the ark rather than in it; Ellicott closes it, holding the statement here decisive and the language of the Epistle a general description of the temple rather than an inventory.

outliers.view: Turns the contents of the ark into an argument about the knowledge of God, that the hallowing of the tables of the Law binds religion and morality indissolubly together and shows God best known not in omnipotence or wisdom but in his moral nature.

themes: nothing in the ark save the two tables
which Moses put there at Horeb

schools.summary: Keil and Delitzsch set the cloud beside the dedication of the tabernacle and give both the same signification, the visible symbol of the gracious presence of God filling the house as a sign that the covenant-God had entered and chosen it, and they correct the misreading the sequence invites, that the cloud drove the priests away, since it did not fill the temple until they had come out; Ellicott identifies it as the bright Shechinah, at once cloud and fire, traces it from Sinai through the tabernacle to the temple and forward through the visions of the prophet to its promised return, and declines the word terror for what the priests felt.

Gill offers three causes for the priests being unable to stand, the darkness the cloud first caused, the light that broke out of it and dazzled them, and the terror it struck their minds with, and supplies from the parallel what was happening in the court, the Levites of Asaph and Heman and Jeduthun with their instruments and a hundred and twenty priests blowing trumpets.

Clarke measures how far the cloud reached, that it filled not only the holy of holies but the whole temple, court and all, and became evident to the people, so that Solomon knew God had honoured the place with his presence.

debates.question: Why could the priests not stand to minister?
debates.positions: Gill names darkness, dazzling light and terror of mind as three possible causes; Ellicott allows the shrinking but refuses to call it terror, holding it was not so much dread of a consuming fire as awe and reverence of an unspeakable glory; Keil and Delitzsch answer the question differently again, that the words mean only that service could not be performed, not that the priests were driven out.

outliers.view: Reads the cloud as a statement about how divine glory must be seen at all, not in the unveiled brightness of heaven but through a cloud of mystery, which is all the eye of man can bear.

themes: the priests could not stand to minister

schools.summary: Henry has Solomon silencing the fears of the priests by reminding them that the cloud is a token of God presence and an indication of favour rather than displeasure, and states the paradox of the dwelling without softening it, that God is light and dwells in light but dwells with men in the thick darkness and makes that his pavilion, because they could not bear the dazzling brightness of his glory.

Ellicott makes the same point a matter of optics, that the description of the cloud as thick darkness in no way contradicts the glory shining through it since human eyes are easily darkened by excess of light, and reports and refuses a conjecture that would emend thick darkness to Jerusalem.
Gill has Solomon perceive by the symbol that the Lord was come to take up his dwelling in the house, and speak these words to the comfort of priests and people in consternation at it.
Clarke supplies the two precedents, the cloud by which God showed himself present in the wilderness and the cloud at the dedication of the tabernacle.

debates.question: Should thick darkness be emended to Jerusalem?
debates.positions: Ellicott reports the conjecture, resting on a single Chaldee version and urged as giving better harmony with the following verse and greater simplicity to the utterance, and refuses it: the Greek of one manuscript and the Latin support the received text, Josephus evidently had it before him, and it is hard to see how the more difficult and more striking reading could have arisen from the flatter one.

outliers.view: Draws a rule of comfort out of the darkness, that nothing is more effectual to reconcile us to dark dispensations than to consider what God hath said and compare his word and works together.

themes: the LORD said he would dwell in the thick darkness
the mystery which veils the presence of God

schools.summary: Henry dramatises the sentence as a legal act, a formal giving of possession, since God by the cloud had come down to take it and Solomon in a few words solemnly gives it him, the house being entirely his own and a settled place for him to abide in for ever, never to be alienated and the ark never to be removed again.

Ellicott supplies the brasen scaffold three cubits high from the other record, so that the king could turn alternately towards the temple and towards the people, holds that the omission in the following verses needs repairing for coherence of idea, and draws out the double parallel between the temporary resting places of the ark and the rulers raised up successively and then removed; Keil and Delitzsch note that the promise is taken freely from the older book rather than quoted, and that the parallel account inserts the clause about choosing Jerusalem which is omitted here.

Clarke supposes the unrecorded blessing to have been the one the high priest pronounced, since Solomon seems here to be acting the high priest part, though he thinks the king may rather have had in view the conduct of Moses and of David; and he reports the claim that thirteen Hebrew words have been lost from this book, while doubting they ever formed part of it.

Gill marks the turn from the people to the Lord and describes the two directions the king faced, and contributes the arithmetic that the bringing out of Egypt was by now about four hundred and eighty-eight years past.

debates.question: Is the text of the blessing defective here?
debates.positions: Ellicott holds that it is and would restore from the fuller version the clause about choosing Jerusalem, without which the affirmation does not answer to the negation; Keil and Delitzsch note the omission without calling it a fault; Clarke reports a scholar who counts thirteen words as lost and disagrees, since they are found in none of the versions here and only help to complete the sense in the other account.

outliers.view: Reads the verse as a conveyance rather than a report, with God saying Surely I come and Solomon answering Amen, so that the building changes hands in a sentence.

themes: I have surely built thee an house
a settled place for thee to abide in for ever
I chose David to be over my people

schools.summary: Keil and Delitzsch note how carefully the approval of David intention is worded, that God approves it as such, and read the claim that the Lord has set up his word as the unpacking of the earlier phrase about fulfilling with his hand; from the sequence they conclude that the ark is declared the kernel and star of the temple, because it was the throne of the glory of God; Ellicott takes the description of the ark as containing the covenant for a window on what a divine covenant is.

Gill describes David purpose in three degrees, that his mind was disposed to it, his heart was set upon it and he had taken up a resolution, supplies Nathan as the channel of the refusal, and keeps the reference of the performed word narrow.

Clarke reasons from the earlier verse that since nothing was in the ark but the two tables, the tables are what is here called the covenant, that is a sign of the covenant, as our Lord calls the cup the new covenant in his blood.

debates.question: What is a covenant with God?
debates.positions: Ellicott defines it against the human kind, denying that it is an undertaking of reciprocal engagements between independent parties, which he calls a monstrous conception of the relation between God and man, and holding that it proceeds simply from God will and begins in free grace, requiring only that men believe and obey; he finds the order stated in the Decalogue itself, which opens with a gift and not a demand.

outliers.view: Infer the whole significance of the building from one clause, that because a place was prepared there for the ark, the ark is the kernel and star of the temple.

themes: it was in the heart of David my father
thou shalt not build the house
I am risen up in the room of David
wherein is the covenant of the LORD

schools.summary: Henry finds it remarkable that the king prayed the prayer himself rather than appointing a priest or a prophet, counts it a sign that he had improved his pious education and that with all his learning he had learnt to pray without a prescribed form, and defends both postures, the kneeling as the most proper posture for prayer and the spread hands as an outward expression of fervour that ought not to be despised or ridiculed.

Clarke shows how common the gesture was, collecting instances from the Psalms and then from the heathen poets, and concluding with the saying of one of them that all men in praying lift up their hands to heaven.

Gill places the king at the altar of burnt offering, takes the altar itself to be typical of Christ through whom all sacrifices of prayer and praise become acceptable, and supplies the brass scaffold from the parallel account.

debates.question: Why did Solomon pray it himself?
debates.positions: Henry treats the fact as a credit and an example, that he was far from thinking it a disparagement to be his own chaplain and the mouth of the assembly, and that in all his glory he never looked so great; the other witnesses record the action without asking the question.

outliers.view: Quotes a poet of his own century against those who would think kneeling beneath them, that kneeling never spoiled silk stocking.

themes: spread forth his hands toward heaven

schools.summary: Keil and Delitzsch explain what the opening acknowledgement is for, that by granting the promised blessing the Lord has proved himself the true and only God, and that this provides the requisite confidence for a prayer sure of an answer; they note that the petition about the throne is put in the same conditional shape in which David had uttered the hope, and that the last of these verses introduces all the petitions that follow rather than repeating the one before it; Ellicott hears in the formula the record of a long education from polytheism to the knowledge of the One only God, and says outright what Solomon citation of the promise leaves out.
Gill puts the contrast narrowly, that God is addressed as their covenant God and Father and so distinguished from all the gods of the Gentiles.

debates.question: What does the promise to David actually guarantee?
debates.positions: Ellicott holds that the larger part of it extends beyond Solomon citation, since it declares that even if the seed of David fall away they shall be chastised but not cast off, a certainty the prophet and the Psalmist compare to the fixity of the ordinances of sun and moon; Keil and Delitzsch keep to the conditional form Solomon quotes and observe that the wording here makes rejection more distinctly a possibility.

outliers.view: Finds in the phrase about keeping covenant and mercy a declaration that mercy is pledged to man as a chief part of the covenant, not merely shown at God pleasure.

themes: there is no God like thee
there shall not fail thee a man

schools.summary: Clarke calls the question full of astonishment, veneration and delight, and takes the plural forms as an invitation to astronomy, reasoning that there are systems and systems of systems, that suns may have been created so far off that their light has not yet reached this earth though travelling at a hundred and ninety thousand miles a second, and that a system created every six days since the foundation of the world would still occupy but a speck in the immensity of space.

Keil and Delitzsch are less interested in the immensity than in what the sentence does inside a prayer, treating it as an intermediate thought with which Solomon meets certain contracted ideas of the gracious presence of God in the temple, and rejecting on that ground both rival constructions of the connecting particle and the claim that a new section begins here.

Gill turns the question into a series of his own and suspects a further reference, that Solomon may have had in view the condescension of the Son of God to tabernacle in human nature, his temple being the figure of that body in which the Godhead dwells.

debates.question: Is this the start of a new section of the prayer?
debates.positions: Keil and Delitzsch deny it, holding the verse an aside within a single continuous petition and arguing that the contrary view rests on an inadmissible rendering of the verb that follows; they connect it back to the plea that God keep the words spoken to David.

outliers.view: Answers a rhetorical question about the heavens with several pages of astronomy, and computes the speed of light and the number of possible worlds to show how little the words exaggerate.

themes: will God indeed dwell on the earth
the heaven of heavens cannot contain thee

schools.summary: Keil and Delitzsch gloss the request that God eyes be open upon the house as a prayer that they be directed there by a special providence, find the ground of the petition inside the verse itself in the clause about the name being there, since the working of God in the place is what makes him attend to prayer offered towards it, and explain the phrase toward this place practically, that Solomon himself was praying in the court facing the temple.

Clarke unfolds the clause about the name into its effects, that God will there show forth his power and glory by enlightening, quickening, pardoning, sanctifying and saving all his sincere worshippers, and makes the direction of prayer a figure of mediation, since both tabernacle and temple were types of our Lord and all prayer must go to God through him.

Gill reads the eyes open toward the house as open toward the people who pray in it, widens the petition to the people of Israel in all succeeding ages, and ascribes the acceptance of prayer to the blood and righteousness and mediation of him whom the temple typified.

debates.question: Why should prayer be directed toward the house?
debates.positions: Keil and Delitzsch answer from the circumstances, that Solomon was praying in the court and facing the temple; Clarke and Gill answer doctrinally, making the direction a figure of mediation, since the temple typified the human nature of Christ in which dwelt all the fulness of the Godhead bodily.

outliers.view: Cannot resist noting, against the words of the prayer itself, that heaven was more properly God dwelling place than the house Solomon had just built for him.

themes: that thine eyes may be open toward this house
hear thou in heaven thy dwelling place

schools.summary: Clarke supplies the frame the rest of the prayer hangs on, that Solomon puts here seven cases in all of which the mercy and intervention of God would be indispensably requisite, and describes the first as a case of doubtfulness in which the accused, there being no direct evidence, purges himself by oath at the altar; he describes the second as defeat and captivity for transgression, and the third as the withholding of the early and latter rain.

Gill fills in the kind of wrong meant in the first case, an unfaithfulness in a trust committed to him or the like, marks that the sin to be forgiven in the second is public and not personal, and notes that heaven may be said to be shut up when the air is quite serene and not a cloud in it.

Keil and Delitzsch anchor the second petition in the threatenings of the law and settle two clauses of the third against rival renderings, the first meaning because thou humblest them rather than that thou hearest them, and the second because thou teachest them the good way.

debates.question: What force do the two clauses in the third case have?
debates.positions: Keil and Delitzsch reject the rendering that thou hearest them and insist on because thou humblest them, pairing it with because thou teachest them the good way; the two together, they argue, contain a motive for forgiveness, since God who chastises in order to teach must forgive when the chastisement is recognised as his and met with penitential prayer.

outliers.view: Organises the whole central section of the prayer by counting seven distinct cases, and numbers each as he reaches it.

themes: an oath come before thine altar

schools.summary: Keil and Delitzsch run through the list of land-plagues with the law open beside them, famine and pestilence and blight and mildew and locusts and oppression by enemies and diseases of every kind, each threatened against the rebellious in the older books, and notice that the word for the devourer is joined to the word for the locust without a connecting particle, which they take for a way of depicting the plague more vividly.

Clarke breaks the same list into nine heads and defines each, from the black offensive dust of blasting to the caterpillar as the locust in its young state, distinguishing locusts brought by winds from other countries from those bred in the land, and locates what makes such prayers acceptable inside the man, since only those who knew the plague of their own hearts were likely to pray in such a manner.

Gill supplies a memory that would make the first item concrete, the three years famine in the time of David, keeps the clause about prayer wide enough to cover any trouble whatever, and reads the closing purpose as gratitude rather than dread, that they may fear him for his goodness in hearing and forgiving.

debates.question: What qualifies a man to make this prayer?
debates.positions: Clarke locates it in self-knowledge, that only those aware of the plague of their own hearts, of the deep-rooted moral corruption of their nature, would pray in such a manner at all; Gill keeps the condition external and wide, covering any prayer on account of any of these things or any other.

outliers.view: Reads the stated end of the petition, that they may fear thee, as produced by kindness rather than by the plagues, arising from the hearing of prayer and the forgiving of sins.

themes: the plague of his own heart

schools.summary: Keil and Delitzsch point out that Solomon assumes as certain that foreigners will come and worship in the temple, note that Moses himself had allowed foreigners living among Israel to sacrifice there, read the verse about what the stranger will have heard as a parenthesis rather than a new clause, and correct the usual readings of the closing phrase about the house being called by God name, holding that the naming of the name presupposes the working of God within and denotes the acknowledgment of that working.

Clarke reads the fifth case as relating to heathens coming from other countries with the design of becoming proselytes, that they might be received and blessed and protected as the true Israelites were, so that the name of God might be known over the face of the earth.

Gill describes the stranger as one of another country having some knowledge of and disposition to the true worship of God, and expands the great name into the eternal, immutable and self-existent Being together with the perfections displayed in his mighty works.

debates.question: What does it mean that the house is called by God name?
debates.positions: Keil and Delitzsch reject both common explanations, that the house is called after his name and that his name was invoked over it at the dedication, arguing from the older passage the phrase is taken from that the name of the Lord always denotes the working of God among his people, so that naming it over a place presupposes that working and confesses it.

outliers.view: Treat the whole verse about the great name and the outstretched arm as a parenthesis explaining a single earlier phrase, and resume the main sentence afterwards.

themes: thy strong hand and thy stretched out arm
that all people of the earth may know

schools.summary: Clarke fastens on the qualifying clause and makes it the whole of the case, that the petition refers to wars undertaken by divine appointment since in no others could they expect the blessing and concurrence of the Lord, and then presses the limitation into his own day, holding that there are no such wars under the Christian dispensation nor can be, that except mere defensive war all others are diabolic, and asking whether without provocations there would be any need of defensive wars at all.

Keil and Delitzsch set out the architecture of the two closing petitions, the sixth for Israel at war by the appointment of God and the seventh for Israel carried away for its sins, and defend the passage against a commentator who argued on doctrinal grounds that these verses are an interpolation, holding it quite in harmony with the original plan that prayer from a distance should be anticipated.

Gill keeps to the circumstances that would make such a war lawful, an enemy threatening invasion or trespassing on their borders or infringing their liberties, and reads the petition as a prayer for success.

debates.question: Do these petitions belong to the original prayer?
debates.positions: Keil and Delitzsch report and reject the claim that they are an interpolated addition made on doctrinal grounds, agreeing with the answer that anticipating prayer offered far from the sanctuary is exactly what the plan of the prayer requires.

outliers.view: Turns a petition about divinely appointed war into a flat denial that any such war is now possible, holding all but defensive war diabolic since the Son of man came to save lives and not destroy them.

themes: if thy people go out to battle
toward the city which thou hast chosen

schools.summary: Clarke infers from the punishment what kind of sin the seventh case supposes, some general defection from truth or species of false worship, since captivity was the general punishment for idolatry, and then quarrels with the received translation of the parenthesis on a point of logic, holding that if no man sinneth not it is useless to say if they sin, and that the original should be rendered there is no man that may not sin.

Keil and Delitzsch refuse the rendering that would make the first phrase of the repentance mean they feel remorse, on the ground that the form cannot carry that reflexive sense, and widen the scope of the petition beyond the exile of the whole nation foretold in the law to every case of transportation into an enemy land, noting that the words of the confession were the very ones afterwards adopted in captivity.

Gill takes the opening clause of the same persons who had gone out to battle in the case before, and describes the turning in two stages, a returning to their heart which remembers the sins that caused the captivity, and a returning to God with great ingenuity and uprightness.

debates.question: Should the parenthesis read there is no man that sinneth not?
debates.positions: Clarke says no, since on that rendering the second clause makes the supposition in the first nugatory; the original should be if they shall sin, for there is no man that may not sin, meaning none impeccable and none infallible, and he shows that the translators themselves render the same word permissively elsewhere, including earlier in this very chapter.

outliers.view: Corrects a familiar proof-text for universal sinfulness on grammatical grounds, arguing that the verse asserts liability to sin rather than the fact of it.

themes: there is no man that sinneth not
we have sinned, and have done perversely
return unto thee with all their heart

schools.summary: Clarke notes what is not asked, that Solomon does not pray for deliverance out of the captivity but that their enemies may use them well and that they may, as formerly, be kept a separate and distinct people.

Keil and Delitzsch give the clause literally, make them for compassion before their captors, that is cause them to meet with compassion from the enemies who carried them away, and supply the image of the furnace of iron; Ellicott traces what became of the petition and finds it answered unevenly, singularly fulfilled at the captivity of Judah in Babylon but not, so far as we hear, in the captivity of the lost tribes in Assyria.

Gill reads the forgiveness asked for as one that would show itself in a return to their own land, takes the request that God eyes be open to cover any supplication Solomon should hereafter make in this place, and resolves the separation of Israel into four acts, the choice, the redemption out of Egypt, the peculiar laws and the special blessings.

debates.question: Was this petition ever answered?
debates.positions: Ellicott holds that it was, and unevenly, pointing to the exceptional favour shown to the Jews in Babylon and still more to the restoration granted by Cyrus and Darius, while noting that nothing of the kind is recorded of the tribes carried into Assyria, and calling the whole course of Jewish fortunes in dispersion unique in history.

outliers.view: Observes that the prayer stops short of asking for release, seeking only good treatment and the preservation of the people as distinct while the captivity lasts.

themes: give them compassion before them who carried them captive

schools.summary: Henry marks the shape of what follows before its content, that as Solomon gives the conclusion of the whole matter after his sermon in one of his books, so he does here after this long prayer, pronouncing it standing that he might be the better heard and because he blessed as one having authority, and judging that never were words more fitly spoken nor a congregation dismissed with what was more likely to abide with them.

Ellicott raises the question whether what was pronounced was a blessing at all, since blessing the congregation was the special duty of the priests while here the king alone is conspicuous, and answers that Solomon words are not strictly of blessing but of praise and prayer to God and exhortation to the people; he also notes what this account omits at this exact point, the kindling of the sacrifice by fire from heaven which the parallel record inserts; Keil and Delitzsch add a point of construction, that the clause about the spread hands is circumstantial and belongs with the words before it.

Gill reads the moment typically, that in praying and interceding for his people before the altar Solomon was a type of Christ, and notes the loud voice and the double office, father of his people and preacher in Jerusalem.

debates.question: Was this a priestly blessing?
debates.positions: Ellicott doubts it, noting that blessing the congregation belonged to the priests while the narrative gives the office to the king alone, and resolving the difficulty by observing that the words are praise and exhortation rather than benediction; Gill and Clarke treat it simply as a benediction, Clarke locating its text in the two verses following.

outliers.view: Points out a whole scene missing from this account at this verse, the fire from heaven and a second manifestation of the glory, which the parallel record supplies.

themes: he arose from before the altar
blessed all the congregation with a loud voice

schools.summary: Henry dwells on what Solomon singles out for thanksgiving, that he began by blessing God and blessed him not for wealth or honour or power or victory but for rest, as if that were a blessing more valuable than any of those, and that the second half of the verse writes a receipt in full on the back of the bonds, declaring that not one word of all the good promises has failed.

Keil and Delitzsch locate the two halves of the praise in two different sets of promises and qualify the word rest historically, since the rest given by Joshua was only fully secured by David victories while parts of the land remained in Canaanite hands; Ellicott carries the word forward to its perfect accomplishment under Solomon the Peaceful and then turns it round, since entering into that rest was conditional on walking in the ways of the Lord, a condition Solomon himself broke.
Gill glosses the rest twice over, as a land of rest and as rest in the land from all enemies.

debates.question: When was the promise of rest fulfilled?
debates.positions: Keil and Delitzsch distinguish stages, a rest given through Joshua at the conquest but only fully secured by David victories; Ellicott makes this reign the first perfect accomplishment and the first thorough entry upon the whole charter of the land, and then adds that the condition attached to it was broken, so that the glory of the age proved a gleam of prosperity soon swallowed up in dissension and disaster.

outliers.view: Ranks rest above the blessings Solomon does not name, and turns it into an admonition that those who have rest should not undervalue it though they want some others.

themes: there hath not failed one word
by the hand of Moses his servant

schools.summary: Gill fills in who the fathers were and what God being with them had meant, to guide and direct, protect and defend, succeed and prosper them, and holds that nothing is more desirable than the presence of God and that Solomon could not have prayed for a greater blessing; he takes the inclining of the heart to be the work of the Spirit, bending them to love and fear and serve God.

Ellicott makes the clause about inclining the heart, set beside the exhortation a few verses later, the occasion for stating the faith he takes to underlie the whole idea of covenant, a faith in the mysterious co-operation of the preventing grace of God with the free responsibility of man, since God inclines the heart and yet the heart must yield itself.
Henry counts the presence of God the first of four things Solomon desires for the people, and calls it all in all to the happiness of a church and a nation.

debates.question: How can God incline a heart that must yield itself?
debates.positions: Ellicott refuses to resolve the tension and calls it the faith pervading all Holy Scripture, arguing that the conviction grows plainer as a man realises the inner life of the soul and the dominion of God over it by grace, and that it is brought out most fully in the covenant of the Spirit, most vividly in the paradox that bids men work out their own salvation because it is God which worketh in them.

outliers.view: Reads a single clause of a dedication prayer as the seed of a doctrine of grace, and traces it through the Psalms and Proverbs and the prophets to its fullest statement afterwards.

themes: the LORD our God be with us
let him not leave us, nor forsake us
that he may incline our hearts unto him

schools.summary: Clarke calls these verses a sort of supplement to the prayer that ended earlier, and quotes in full the important addition the parallel place contains, the petition that the Lord arise into his resting place with the ark of his strength; on the closing exhortation he is brief, that they be sincere in their faith and irreproachable in their conduct.

Keil and Delitzsch render the request closely, that these words be near to the Lord day and night so that he may secure the right of the king and of his people as every day demands, note that the words meant are the petitions already offered, and take the perfect heart to be one wholly and undividedly devoted to the Lord.

Gill lists the ways in which all the people of the earth would come to know that the Lord is God, by his chastising Israel when they sinned, hearing and answering their prayers, forgiving their sins, delivering them out of troubles and protecting them in their blessings, and resolves the perfect heart into sincerity in love, unitedness in worship and constancy in obedience.

debates.question: What is the end for which the prayer is offered?
debates.positions: Gill and Keil and Delitzsch both read the stated purpose outward rather than inward, that all the people of the earth may know that the Lord is God and that there is none else, Gill listing the dealings with Israel through which that knowledge would come.

outliers.view: Supplies from the parallel account a closing petition missing here altogether, that the priests be clothed with salvation and the face of the anointed not turned away.

themes: let these my words be nigh unto the LORD
that all the people of the earth may know

schools.summary: Keil and Delitzsch report the numbers of the thank-offering and an attempt to set them aside as too large by a calculation of how many beasts a minute would have to be killed, answering that the calculation holds only if the whole number was for the king alone, if none but priests and Levites could slaughter, and if all the flesh was to be burnt; Ellicott insists the real difficulty has been mislocated, since bringing and consuming such a mass is easy to conceive given the multitude assembled, while offering it even over fourteen days is not, and suggests that representative victims of each hundred were sacrificed and the rest simply dedicated.

Henry does not dispute the figures but sets them beside two other occasions, the hecatombs of the heathen and the far smaller offerings at the dedication of the altar in the wilderness when the people were poor, and draws the comparison that thirty oxen a day served Solomon own table while thousands went to God altar, few being minded to spend more upon their souls than upon their bodies.

Gill takes the total to cover all fourteen days and describes the court of the priests hallowed in its middle part for present use; Clarke agrees on the fourteen days and asks how they could possibly have disposed of the blood of so many victims.

debates.question: Are the numbers credible?
debates.positions: Keil and Delitzsch defend them by dismantling the assumptions behind the objection; Ellicott accepts them as textually certain, being reproduced in the parallel account and by Josephus, and relocates the difficulty from consumption to the physical act of offering, proposing that most of the beasts were dedicated rather than sacrificed at the altar.

debates.question: What does the profusion signify?
debates.positions: Henry takes it as generosity proportioned to increased wealth, on the rule that where God sows plentifully he must reap accordingly; Ellicott suspects something worse mixed in, the heathen notion that the Lord would be pleased with thousands of rams, and a display of royal magnificence in the very act of homage, in which he thinks lurked the evils that were to overthrow Israel.

outliers.view: Uses the silence about the priests, even in the hallowing of the court, as evidence about the narrator rather than the ceremony, since the king alone is prominent throughout this account.

themes: an hundred and twenty thousand sheep
hallowed the middle of the court
the brasen altar was too little

schools.summary: Keil and Delitzsch read the two limits as covering the whole land in its fullest extent from north to south; Ellicott identifies the northern limit as the great valley between the two ranges, the main entrance to Palestine from the north down which the hosts of Assyria and Babylon so constantly poured, and corrects a natural mistake about the southern, that the river of Egypt is not the Nile nor any of its branches but the torrent identified by all authorities with the one falling into the sea at El-Arish.

Clarke names both ends differently, taking the first for Antioch of Syria and the second for the Rhinocorura while reaching the same conclusion, and closes on the mood of the people, that they were contented with their king, at peace among themselves and happy in their God, before adding that the king fell and the nation followed his example.

Gill takes the king contribution to the feast to be both his own portion of the peace offerings and whatever he might as a liberal prince provide besides, and is exact about the day of dismissal while admitting that by the other account they did not actually go until the twenty-third.

debates.question: Where are the two limits of the gathering?
debates.positions: Ellicott places the northern limit in the valley between the two ranges and insists the southern is a torrent rather than the Nile; Clarke identifies them as a Syrian city and a coastal town instead, but draws the same conclusion, that the phrase means from one extremity of the land to the other.

outliers.view: Ends the chapter on a reversal, that so contented and prosperous a people would have remained so had their king continued to walk uprightly, but the king fell and the nation followed him.

themes: from the entering in of Hamath
